content: The text provided is a list of references formatted in a specific citation style. It includes details about various studies, trials, reviews, and guidelines related to neonatal and maternal health, vitamin supplementation, breastfeeding, postnatal care, and other related topics. 1. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted in Ghana (Neovita) evaluated the effects of neonatal vitamin A supplementation on infant mortality. The findings were published in The Lancet in 2015 (Volume 385, Issue 9975, Pages 1315–1323). 2. Masanja et al. investigated the impact of neonatal vitamin A supplementation on infant mortality in Tanzania through a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Neovita). The results were published in The Lancet in 2015 (Volume 385, Issue 9975, Pages 1324–1332). 3. Mazumder et al. assessed the efficacy of early neonatal vitamin A supplementation in reducing infant mortality in Haryana, India, through a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Neovita). The study was published in The Lancet in 2015 (Volume 385, Issue 9975, Pages 1333–1342). 4. Ahmad et al. explored the transient effects of high-dose neonatal vitamin A supplementation on thymic function during early infancy. The findings were published in The Journal of Nutrition in 2020 (Volume 150, Issue 1, Pages 176–183). 5. Klemm et al. tested the feasibility of delivering vitamin A to newborns in Nepal and Bangladesh. The results were published in Sight and Life in 2011 (Volume 25, Pages 30–37). 6. The Codex Alimentarius Commission established a global standard for infant formula and formulas for special medical purposes intended for infants. This standard, originally adopted in 1981, was updated by the World Health Organization in 2007. 7. Tan et al. reviewed the role of vitamin D supplementation in term breastfed infants to prevent vitamin D deficiency and improve bone health. This systematic review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2020 (Issue 12, Article CD013046). 8. The World Health Organization (WHO) provided recommendations on optimal feeding practices for low birth-weight infants in lowand middle-income countries in 2011, emphasizing maternal and newborn care for a positive postnatal experience. 9. Chandy et al. conducted a randomized placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation, either directly or via breast milk, on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels, related biochemistry, and infection susceptibility in term infants. The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition in 2016 (Volume 116, Issue 1, Pages 52–58). 10. Floreskul et al. performed a modeling study to assess the cost-effectiveness of vitamin D supplementation in pregnant women and young children for the prevention of rickets. The findings were published in Frontiers in Public Health in 2020 (Volume 8, Article 439). 11. Roth et al. outlined the global prevalence and disease burden of vitamin D deficiency, providing a roadmap for action in lowand middle-income countries. This comprehensive review was published in Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences in 2018 (Volume 1430, Issue 1, Pages 44–79). 12. Wagner and Greer discussed strategies for the prevention of rickets and vitamin D deficiency in infants, children, and adolescents. Their recommendations were published in Pediatrics in 2008 (Volume 122, Issue 5, Pages 1142–1152). 13. Simon and Ahrens examined adherence to vitamin D intake guidelines in the United States, with their findings published in Pediatrics in 2020 (Volume 145, Issue 6, Article e20193574). 14. Umaretiya et al. explored maternal preferences for vitamin D supplementation in breastfed infants. Their study was published in Annals of Family Medicine in 2017 (Volume 15, Issue 1, Pages 68–70). 15. Taylor et al. investigated the use of supplemental vitamin D among infants breastfed for prolonged periods. The results were published in Pediatrics in 2010 (Volume 125, Issue 1, Pages 105–111). 16. Heinig reviewed controversies and concerns surrounding vitamin D supplementation in breastfed infants. This review was published in Journal of Human Lactation in 2003 (Volume 19, Issue 3, Pages 247–249). 17. The Vitamin D Expert Panel released a final report summarizing their findings and recommendations, which was accessed on January 20, 2022. 18. Crocker et al. reported very high rates of vitamin D supplementation among infants aged two months in Vancouver and Richmond, British Columbia, Canada. The study was published in BMC Public Health in 2011 (Volume 11, Article 905). 19. Gallo et al. examined vitamin D supplementation practices among Canadian infants, focusing on the behaviors of mothers in Montreal. The findings were published in Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism in 2010 (Volume 35, Issue 3, Pages 303–309). 20. Hemingway et al. assessed adherence to infant vitamin D supplementation policies in Ireland. The study was published in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2020 (Pages 1337–1345). 21. Field conducted a narrative review of pediatric massage therapy research, highlighting its benefits. This review was published in Children (Basel) in 2019 (Volume 6, Issue 6). 22. Kulkarni et al. reviewed the current evidence on massage and touch therapy in neonates, with their findings published in Indian Pediatrics in 2010 (Volume 47, Pages 771–776). 23. Diego and Field demonstrated that moderate-pressure massage elicits a parasympathetic nervous system response. Their study was published in the International Journal of Neuroscience in 2009 (Volume 119, Issue 5, Pages 630–638). 24. Schanberg et al. found that massage with oil has more positive effects on normal infants compared to massage without oil. This study was published in the Journal of Prenatal and Perinatal Psychology and Health in 1996 (Volume 11, Issue 2, Page 75). 25. Field reviewed research on massage therapy, summarizing its clinical applications and benefits. This review was published in Complementary Therapies in Clinical Practice in 2016 (Volume 24, Pages 19–31). 26. Priyadarshi et al. conducted a systematic review to evaluate the effects of whole-body massage on growth and neurodevelopment in term healthy newborns. The findings are currently under review. 27. Bennett et al. reviewed the role of massage in promoting mental and physical health in typically developing infants under six months of age. This review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2013 (Issue 4, Article CD005038). 28. Zhang et al. performed a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to assess the influence of massage on neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. The study was published in the Journal of Maternal-Fetal & Neonatal Medicine in 2019 (Volume 32, Issue 18, Pages 3109–3114). 29. Gürol and Polat investigated the effects of baby massage on attachment between mothers and their infants. Their findings were published in Asian Nursing Research in 2012 (Volume 6, Issue 1, Pages 35–41). 30. Keller and Rehm conducted a qualitative case study exploring fathers' experiences of massaging their infants. The study was published in the Journal of Behavioral and Social Sciences in 2015 (Volume 2, Pages 29–39). 31. The World Health Organization released guidelines in 2020 aimed at improving early childhood development through evidence-based interventions. 32. The WHO and UNICEF outlined acceptable medical reasons for the use of breast-milk substitutes in a 2009 publication.
